terms.gloss: a grade, a mark for schoolwork
terms.comment: Classically any mark or sign, among them the critic’s mark set against a bad line (notam appōnere ad malum versum, Cic. Pis. 73) and the brand on a wine jar, whence a grade of quality: secundae notae mel, second-grade honey (Col. 9.15.3, Lewis & Short). To grade papers is notāre (Traupman 29).

evidence: M-O s.v. grade: quot pūncta tulistī?, what grade did you get?
terms.comment: Classically the dot that tallied a vote on a wax tablet, and so a vote (Lewis & Short); hence Horace’s omne tulit pūnctum, ‘he has carried every vote’, which Morgan–Owens turns into full marks: omne pūnctum ferre.
Classically to mark or note; Traupman also gives aestimāre, to assess.

phrases.latin: omne tulit pūnctum quī miscuit ūtile dulcī
phrases.english: he has carried every vote who has mixed the useful with the sweet

sources: Lewis & Short: nota · Lewis & Short: noto · Lewis & Short: punctum
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. grade.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 29, 323.
